source_text:
propterea autem commemoramus, quibus eiusmodi loca dicentur, ut eorum demonstremus esse quae in iis locis fiunt, quibus ipsa loca dicantur.,
Nunc de artificio quo circenses exhibentur. res equestris retro simplex: de dorso agebatur, et utique communis usus; reus non erat. sed cum ad ludos coactus est, transiit a dei munere ad daemoniorum officia. itaque Castori et Polluci deputatur, haec species, quibus equos a Mercurio distributos Stesichorus docet. sed et Neptunus equestris est, quem Graeci ἵππιον appellant. seiugas uero Ioui, quadrigas Soli, bigas Lunae sanxerunt. sed et Primus Erichthonius currus et quattuor ausus Iungere equos rapidusque rotis insistere uictor. Erichthonius, Mineruae et Vulcani filius, et quidem de caduca in terram libidine, portentum est daemonicum, immo diabolus ipse, non coluber. si uero Trochilus Argiuus auctor est currus, primae Iunoni id opus suum dedicauit. si Romae Romulus quadrigam primus ostendit, puto et ipse inter idola conscriptus est, si idem est Quirinus. talibus auctoribus quadrigae productae merito et aurigas coloribus idololatriae uestierunt. namque initio duo soli fuerunt, albus et russeus. albus hiemi ob niues candidas, russeus aestati ob solis ruborem uoti erantsed postea tam uoluptate quam superstitione prouecta russeum alii Marti, alii album Zephyris consecrauerunt, prasinum uero Terrae matri uel uerno, uenetum Caelo et Mari uel autumno. cum autem omnis species idololatriae damnata sit a deo, utique etiam illa damnatur, quae elementis mundialibus profanatur.
thought_title: The chariot and its colors are demonic inventions
orientation: Tertullian is tracing the origins of the circus, now turning from the places to the art of chariot-racing itself.
pass_a_gloss: But for this reason we call to mind the things to which places of this kind are said to belong, so that we may show that the things which happen in those places belong to those to whom the places themselves are said to belong. Now about the art by which circus shows are exhibited. The equestrian activity was formerly simple: it was done from the back, and certainly it was common use; it was not a defendant. But when it was forced into the games, it passed from a gift of God to services of demons. And so this kind is assigned to Castor and Pollux, to whom Stesichorus teaches that horses were distributed by Mercury. But Neptune also is equestrian, whom the Greeks call hippion. But they consecrated the six-horse chariots to Jupiter, the four-horse chariots to the Sun, the two-horse chariots to the Moon. But also Erichthonius first dared to yoke chariots and four horses and to stand on wheels as swift victor. Erichthonius, son of Minerva and Vulcan, and indeed from lust fallen to the ground, is a demonic portent, or rather the devil himself, not a snake. But if Trochilus the Argive is the author of the chariot, he dedicated this work of his to first Juno. If at Rome Romulus first displayed the four-horse chariot, I think he too has been enrolled among the idols, if he is the same as Quirinus. With such authors were the four-horse chariots produced, and deservedly they clothed the charioteers also with the colors of idolatry. For at the beginning there were only two, white and red. White was vowed to winter because of the white snows, red to summer because of the redness of the sun. But afterwards, as much by pleasure as by superstition having been advanced, some consecrated the red to Mars, others the white to the Zephyrs, the green indeed to Mother Earth or to spring, the blue to Sky and Sea or to autumn. But since every kind of idolatry has been condemned by God, certainly also that is condemned which is profaned by the elements of the world.

choices.why: Keeps the legal metaphor literally; Tertullian means riding was not on trial, not accused of any crime.

choices.term: transiit a dei munere ad daemoniorum officia
choices.english: it passed from a gift of God to services of demons
choices.why: Preserves the contrast between God's gift and demonic service, and the verb of motion.
rejected: it went from being God's gift to being the demons' work

choices.term: portentum est daemonicum, immo diabolus ipse, non coluber
choices.english: is a demonic portent, or rather the devil himself, not a snake
choices.why: Keeps the correction 'or rather' and the blunt identification with the devil, not just a snake.
rejected: is a demonic monster, indeed the devil himself, not a serpent

choices.why: Preserves the passive of 'uoueo' and the idea of dedication by vow.

choices.english: as much by pleasure as by superstition having been advanced
choices.why: Keeps the ablative of means and the perfect passive participle; the colors were advanced, i.e., increased, by both motives.
rejected: advanced by both pleasure and superstition

choices.english: is profaned by the elements of the world
choices.why: Keeps the passive and the phrase 'elements of the world,' which echoes Pauline language.

pass_b_english: We recall the places so named for this reason: to show that what happens in them belongs to the beings for whom the places themselves are named.

Now for the art by which the circus shows are presented. Riding was once a simple matter. A man rode on the horse's back, and it was ordinary, everyday use. It was no crime. But when riding was forced into the games, it passed from a gift of God into the service of demons.

So this kind of riding is assigned to Castor and Pollux. The Greek poet Stesichorus teaches that their horses were distributed to them by Mercury. Neptune too is a god of horses; the Greeks call him Hippios, the Horseman. They consecrated the single-horse chariot to Jupiter, the four-horse chariot to the Sun, and the two-horse chariot to the Moon.

Erichthonius was the first who dared to yoke four horses to a chariot and stand victorious on swift wheels. Now Erichthonius, the son of Minerva and Vulcan, born from lust that fell to the earth, is a demonic portent. Or rather, he is the devil himself, not a mere snake. If Trochilus the Argive is the inventor of the chariot, he dedicated his work to Juno first. If Romulus first displayed a four-horse chariot at Rome, I think he too has been enrolled among the idols, if he is the same as Quirinus.

With such founders the four-horse chariots were produced, and rightly the charioteers clothed themselves in the colors of idolatry. For at first there were only two colors, white and red. White was vowed to winter because of the white snows, red to summer because of the sun's redness. But later, as much by pleasure as by superstition, they advanced further. Some consecrated red to Mars, others white to the West Winds, green to Mother Earth or to spring, and blue to Sky and Sea or to autumn.
But since every kind of idolatry has been condemned by God, certainly that too is condemned which is profaned by the elements of the world.

problems.quote: Now for the art by which the circus shows are exhibited.
problems.source_quote: propterea autem commemoramus, quibus eiusmodi loca dicentur, ut eorum demonstremus esse quae in iis locis fiunt, quibus ipsa loca dicantur.
problems.why: The opening clause explaining why the places are mentioned is omitted, losing the introductory purpose.
problems.fix: Therefore we recall the places so named, to show that what occurs there is what they are called; now about the art by which the circus shows are exhibited.
problems.ruling: Source sentence 'propterea autem commemoramus...dicantur' is entirely omitted, losing the stated purpose of the discussion.

problems.why: ‘reus’ means ‘guilty’ or ‘a crime’, not ‘defendant’; the translation reverses the sense.
problems.ruling: 'reus non erat' means 'it was not guilty/a crime'; 'defendant' misleads reader by shifting legal sense.

edits.old: Now for the art by which the circus shows are exhibited.
edits.new: Therefore we recall the places so named, to show that what occurs there is what they are called; now about the art by which the circus shows are exhibited.

fixed: The opening clause was omitted; restored it.

problems.quote: two-horse chariots to Jupiter, four-horse chariots to the Sun, and two-horse chariots to the Moon
problems.source_quote: seiugas uero Ioui, quadrigas Soli, bigas Lunae sanxerunt
problems.why: bigas is two-horse, but seiugas is single-horse (one-yoke) chariots, not two-horse.
problems.fix: single-horse chariots to Jupiter, four-horse chariots to the Sun, and two-horse chariots to the Moon
problems.ruling: source 'seiugas' = single‑horse chariots, not two‑horse; translation says 'two‑horse chariots', altering meaning

edits.old: They consecrated two-horse chariots to Jupiter, four-horse chariots to the Sun, and two-horse chariots to the Moon.
edits.new: They consecrated single-horse chariots to Jupiter, four-horse chariots to the Sun, and two-horse chariots to the Moon.

fixed: Changed 'two-horse chariots to Jupiter' to 'single-horse chariots to Jupiter' because the source 'seiugas' means single-horse (one-yoke) chariots, not two-horse.

last_rejected.quote: White was vowed to winter because of the white snows, red to summer because of the sun's redness.
last_rejected.source_quote: albus hiemi ob niues candidas, russeus aestati ob solis ruborem uoti erant
last_rejected.why: Subject is the colors (albus/russeus), not seasons; 'voti erant' is plural past tense, not singular.
last_rejected.fix: White and red were vowed to winter and summer, the one for the white snows, the other for the sun's redness.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin has colors as subjects; translation says "White was vowed to winter... red to summer..." which matches the source.

polish.changed: Clarified the argument's logic, identified Erichthonius's demonic identity before the snake contrast, explained the Greek epithet Hippios, and smoothed sentence order and pronoun references for modern readers.

variants.text: Erichthonius, the son of Minerva and Vulcan
a demonic portent, or rather the devil himself

notes.why: Tertullian's allegorical identification is jarring without warning.
notes.fix: Note that Tertullian interprets myth as demonic.

notes.quote: the boxing glove itself is a serpentine force
notes.why: 'Serpentine force' is bizarre; caestus as snake-like?

notes.quote: Erichthonius, the son of Minerva and Vulcan, and indeed born from lust that fell to the earth, is a demonic portent, or rather the devil himself, not a snake
notes.why: The final 'not a snake' is confusing; Erichthonius was part-serpent in myth, but the sentence contradicts itself.
notes.fix: Rewrite: 'is a demonic portent—or rather, the devil himself in serpent form.'

notes.why: Greek epithet untranslated; reader does not know it means 'horseman' or 'equestrian.'
notes.fix: Gloss as 'whom the Greeks call Hippios, that is, the Horseman.'

polish.changed: Clarified the identity of Stesichorus as a Greek poet, made the sequence of consecrations easier to follow, and smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and reference.

notes.why: Stesichorus is an ancient Greek poet not identified.
A figure from Greek myth not identified beyond the brief genealogy given.
notes.fix: The genealogy 'son of Minerva and Vulcan' suffices.

notes.why: An obscure mythological inventor not identified.
notes.fix: Add 'a mythical inventor' before the name.

notes.why: Quirinus is the deified Romulus not explained; reader may not connect them.
